new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (34 pp., LD&C 13, hdl 10125/24796, CC BY-NC 4.0, text layer present). extracted text page 11 (printed p. 11, end of sec. 2 'Phonology', immediately after Table 7) reads: "As can be observed from the lexical items throughout this paper, stress is unpre-dictable in Remontado, and presumed to be phonemic as in Tagalog and a number of other major Philippine languages, although no minimal pairs for stress were recorded." Identical to the reported quote apart from the line-break hyphen in 'unpredictable'. Page 4 fn. 9 confirms the diacritic conventions (acute = stress, no glottal; grave = unstressed ultima + final glottal; circumflex = final stress + final glottal), and p. 7 sec. 1.2 confi…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is lexically specified (unpredictable) and treated as phonemic, on the Tagalog model; the cited forms show stress on either the penult or the ultima (e.g. /gitˈnaʔ/ 'middle', /ˈnajun/ 'Nayon', /balagˈhadiʔ/ 'rainbow', /laŋdaˈpan/ 'listen'), with no rule given for which syllable it falls on.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the authors note that no minimal pairs for stress were actually recorded, so phonemic status is presumed rather than demonstrated.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level; words and phrases for the description were recorded in isolation in citation form (p. 7). Orthographic acute = stress without final glottal stop, circumflex = final stress + final glottal stop, grave = unstressed ultima with final glottal stop (p. 4 fn. 9).
new_statements.identity_note: Lobel & Surbano 2019 describe the language of the Remontado (Dumagat) communities of General Nakar (Quezon) and Tanay (Rizal), which they call Hatang-Kayi/Remontado; this is the same language listed in Glottolog as Hatang Kayi remo1247 (ISO agv, Ethnologue 'Remontado Dumagat') and called 'Sinauna (Tagalog)' by Santos 1975, Reid 1994 and Himes 2012. The article notes the Ethnologue/older-literature names are exonyms; no distinct dialect is singled out.

new_statements.relation_note: This audio-embedded edition carries the identical stress paragraph, on the same page (p. 11), as the no-audio edition already quoted in existing_statements; it adds nothing new on stress (only page-count and line-break differences, 35 vs 34 pp.). It supports filling the catalog's empty 'rule' field with lexical/unpredictable stress.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is not predictable from the shape of the word and is treated as lexically specified (phonemic), as in Tagalog; the authors record no minimal pairs. The examples on pp. 9-11 show stress on either the final syllable (e.g. pitû /piˈtuʔ/ 'stomach', baláy /baˈlaj/ 'house') or the penult (e.g. sálu /ˈsalu/ 'river', úbun /ˈubun/ 'child', páray /ˈparaj/), and morphological reduplication keeps the root's stress (Table 5, p. 10). Orthography (p. 4 fn. 9): acute = stress without final glottal stop, grave = unstressed ultima with final glottal stop, circumflex = final stress plus final glottal stop.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; the authors note that no minimal pairs for stress were recorded, so the phonemic status is presumed rather than demonstrated. Recordings were made 'in isolation in citation form' (p. 7).
new_statements.identity_note: The work describes Remontado, also called Hatang-Kayi (earlier 'Sinauna' / 'Remontado Dumagat'), the language of the Remontado ethnolinguistic group of the Rizal-Quezon area of Luzon, drawn from the authors' lexical database with a single speaker's citation-form recordings; it is the same variety the catalog entry refers to. Lobel & Surbano note (p. 8 fn. 18) that Lobel 2013:74 mistakenly wrote some Remontado forms with /o/; this concerns vowels, not stress.
